extracted.intended_audience: aspiring newspaper reporters, correspondents, and copy editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing feature stories, conducting correspondence work for newspapers, and handling copy according to a newspaper style-book. Covers story types, news judgment, transmission methods, deadlines, and technical copy conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational feature type and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Informational features cover subjects like inventions, discoveries, lives of notable people, methods, explanations, and factual accounts; timeliness is not essential but valuable, especially for seasonal topics (Halloween, Christmas, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose topics such as new inventions, biographies, methods, and explanatory pieces; timeliness adds value but is not required. Examples: 'Why Hot Water Dissolves Things', holiday-appropriate pieces. ''Timeliness is not essential, but is valuable.''

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources can be anywhere — street, club, church, court, athletic field, reference books, government publications, fashion journals, travelers, old settlers, and local residents; the only requirement is personal observation and investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine diverse local and documentary sources; use portraits/photographs of subjects when available; collect reminiscences and first-person material. Emphasize firsthand observation and investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form is flexible; use attention-getting leads
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature story has no fixed form; the writer is free to begin in any way likely to attract the reader, with informal leads common — give enough to excite curiosity without revealing all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal or suspensive leads to arrest attention. Examples provided (e.g., 'SAM DREAMS OF ROBBERS', 'FIXES BROKEN LEG WITH NAILS'). Aim to arrest attention and hold curiosity rather than follow a rigid inverted pyramid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense story construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some features maintain a suspensive narrative throughout, keeping the reader in suspense until resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain suspense by structuring events and revelations so curiosity is prolonged; use instalment-like reveals or progressive disclosures as shown in 'MISSOURI' IN CHICAGO example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unique style or form
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may employ a unique form or style to achieve effect and attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resort to distinctive forms or compact, epigrammatic paragraphs (example: 'mS WIFE, SHE WENT AWAY' vignette) when it serves the story's effect; uniqueness can substitute for factual novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of impression/tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Most feature stories aim for unity of impression by adhering closely to a single tone or effect (e.g., pathos, humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent tone throughout to produce a coherent impression; the cited Frank Ward O'Malley story is an example of a unified tone of pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate assignment of feature writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature stories are usually written by regular staff writers, contributors, or specialists; strong feature men often write human-interest pieces on a regular basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign features to staff or specialists who can handle the tone and depth required. Beginners are advised to try human-interest features to gain experience and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent's need for news discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents are relatively unsupervised and must be discriminating in judging what is of interest to the home paper; they need the 'nose for news' to tell national vs. local interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentally place yourself in the readers' locale (e.g., Boston, Atlanta) to judge interest; avoid sending items that are only locally meaningful unless they have broader significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating the worth of a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether an item of local news would interest readers who know nothing of the local context; only send if it has broader relevance or unusual qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the story would interest a distant reader; examples contrast a petty blacksmith accident (not worth sending) vs. a bomb-making revelation (worth sending). Tailor judgment to the receiving paper's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: What not to send
rubrics_metrics.description: Never send merely local items such as minor accidents, burglaries, robberies, obituaries, marriages, small entertainments, court trials of little-known persons, murders of obscure persons (unless unusual), county fairs, fraternal meetings, local picnics, ordinary crop/weather items, praise/press-agent stories, tasteless material, or unverified local gossip affecting reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress items trespassing good taste; verify potentially defamatory local gossip before sending. Sensational news should be carefully investigated before transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rumors and potentially libelous items
rubrics_metrics.description: Rumors of sensational news should not be held too long for verification; if non-libelous, send immediately labeled as a rumor; if libelous, notify editors 'Private, not for publication' while investigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP guidance: announce rumors as rumors with investigation note; if accusations might be libelous, use private bulletins for editors rather than public dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to send (tailor to paper's specialties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Send big news and items that match the receiving paper's characteristic interests (freak news, sporting news, educational news, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the paper's columns to learn its specialties; different papers pay for or value different beats (e.g., one wants every Fourth of July injury, another wants college sports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conducting a local column
rubrics_metrics.description: When running a local column, never imply there is little news; use local reminiscences, humorous incidents, and feature stories to fill space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek unnumbered local sources (old settlers, Civil War recollections, weather anecdotes) and present features directly relevant to community life to keep readers engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sending stories by mail — when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the mail for stories where timing is not critical (feature stories, advance speeches, elections) and for advance manuscripts; ensure mail arrival by the paper's deadline or use special delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mail is acceptable if certain of arrival by 10:00 a.m. for afternoons or 8:00 p.m. for mornings; use special delivery and wire when sending important photographs; specify release times for advance speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the telephone effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Only use the telephone when mail is too slow or telegraph is inconvenient; do not call with a jumble of facts — sketch or have the story written before dictation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise dictation to minimize long-distance tolls; have the story sketched on paper or written before calling to save time and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the telegraph for immediacy and queries
rubrics_metrics.description: The telegraph is for immediate stories; send a concise 'query' that bulletins the news and states probable length and filing time (e.g., 'Otto Thomson... killed... Four hundred. 8:35 P.M.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the query specific (names, facts, proposed word count, time) rather than blind or vague statements. The query tells the editor whether to publish immediately and what to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing the story while waiting for reply
rubrics_metrics.description: While awaiting the editor's reply to a query, begin writing the story and place the most important details first so the piece can be shortened from the end if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the piece so that if asked for fewer words you can 'kill' only the final paragraphs; do not skeletonize text to save telegram costs—savings are not worth extra editing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obeying editor's word-limit reply
rubrics_metrics.description: If the editor replies with a requested word count (e.g., 'Rush three hundred banker's death'), keep strictly within that limit; sending more can bring reprimand or dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect word limits; edit ruthlessly to fit the requested length and send the first portion if needed. Practice concise writing to meet imposed constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting no reply
rubrics_metrics.description: If no reply is received, assume the story is not wanted (covered by wire services, bulletin was sufficient, or space crowded out); do not be unduly discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reasons such as AP/UP coverage, sufficient bulletin, or later breaking news that displaced your item; learn from such occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing hours and edition deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect edition cut-off times: for afternoon papers be with operator by 9:00 A.M. (noon edition), 12:00 m. (3 p.m.), 2:00 P.M. (5 p.m.); morning papers may accept until 2:00 a.m. but practically close after midnight. Use N.P.R. for late news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know and meet the distinct deadlines for each edition; mark late items N.P.R. (night press rate) so they will be sent after 6:00 p.m. when telegraph rates fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulletining big news immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: When big or unusual news breaks, bulletin a lead immediately with probable length and time (example bulletin about lynching with length and timestamp) and follow with instalments without waiting for a reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If near press time, follow with instalments labeled 'More' and the final as '30'; editors prefer having too much material rather than risking delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sending detailed instalments and telegraph signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Send instalments of a developing story marked 'More' except the last, which is marked '30'; include time and signature and use telegrapher's signals for completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each instalment should be concise and timestamped; example instalments provided for the Frank lynching piece show 'More. 8:45 p.m. Sherman' and final 'Thirty. 9:15. Sherman'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting news standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain absolute impartiality in sporting controversies; file afternoon scores by 7:30 p.m. (8:00 p.m. outside limit); ensure accuracy of box scores and verify any claimed records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid editorializing; verify new records before telegraphing—if in doubt, report as 'what is said to be a record.' Avoid sending minor local contests of limited interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — forwarding time stories and manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward time stories, advance manuscripts, cuts, etc., by mail; express companies may not deliver at night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mail for non-urgent but time-specified materials, ensuring arrival aligns with the paper's release schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — telegram formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In telegrams spell out round numbers and mark the beginning of speeches with 'quote' and the end with 'end quote'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these telegraphic conventions to ensure correct presentation and minimize ambiguity in transmitted text.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — maintain telegraph operator relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep telegraph companies informed of your street address and telephone number and maintain friendly relations with operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators can provide valuable assistance; accurate contact info prevents delivery issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — finish incomplete stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When a preliminary dispatch is filed on an evolving story, follow up and clear up the eventual outcome so the paper is not left in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return results and updates to avoid leaving the paper with unresolved or misleading early copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — accurate location reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting fires, accidents, disasters, etc., locate the scene as accurately as possible, referencing well-known buildings or landmarks as well as street location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use landmarks in addition to street addresses to help editors and readers precisely identify scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — pursue big stories even at expense
rubrics_metrics.description: When a big story breaks, pursue it vigorously even if expenses are required; papers will generally pay reasonable expenses for valuable news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to incur costs to obtain important material; editors will reimburse reasonable expenditures for significant reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — value of timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every minute has value; timely transmission of news increases its worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize prompt filing and use the fastest available transmission appropriate to importance and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction — keep clips and proof of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Until you receive your first payment, clip and keep every story printed; some papers require sending a 'string' of pasted stories for monthly accounting; payment often based on columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain records of published stories for payment and accounting; column rates vary and papers differ in bookkeeping practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style-book: consult and follow local copy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy must be written according to the individual style rules of each newspaper; a reporter's first task in a new office is to ask for and study the style-book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the style-book contains idiosyncratic or odd rules, follow them precisely; when in doubt consult the manual rather than relying on the paper's columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must know how to handle a typewriter dexterously because copy is usually prepared on machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to type quickly and accurately; longhand is rarely sent and will often be typed by staff if received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longhand copy conventions for legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing longhand, be painstakingly legible; print unusual proper names letter by letter; underscore/overscore potentially confusable letters; use half-circle marks for quotation marks and special marks for periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply disambiguation techniques (underscoring, overscoring, special punctuation) to prevent copying errors when a typewriter is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper and stationery standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unglazed paper of neutral tint (gray, yellow, manila brown), commonly unruled print paper 6 x 9 or 8½ x 11 inches and of sufficient firmness to permit ink or pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer office-supplied stationery when available; choose neutral, durable paper suitable for typing and mailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins and pagination of copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave the top half of the first page blank for headlines; include a one-inch margin at bottom and sides on all sheets; non-first sheets should have a one-inch top margin for paging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Margins permit headline writing, corrections, pasting of sheets, and paging. Put the writer's name in a ring at the extreme left corner of the first page.
